q: Would a super-Gaussian or measured-tabular Λ(λ) (digitized from the paper's Fig. 2 at 1-nm resolution) close the systematic ~2× gap between our first-principles reproduction of Eqs. (1)-(4) and the paper's Fig. 6, or would it reveal a hidden dependence in Eq. (3)?
basis: Fitting a Gaussian Λ(λ) to three paper-quoted averages (peak 0.259, mean over ±28.15 nm = 0.20, mean over ±53 nm = 0.129) exactly matches all three constraints yet the resulting Fig-6 key rates come in ~0.46-0.56× the paper's numbers across all five WDM scenarios. The bias is systematic in one direction, suggesting the true Λ(λ) has more area in the shoulders than a Gaussian.
next_steps: Digitize Fig. 2 from the PDF at 1-nm resolution using a plot-tracer (e.g. WebPlotDigitizer), refit Λ as a super-Gaussian or piecewise-linear function, and rerun the pipeline. Compare per-channel contribution to ΣR_s. If the gap doesn't close, examine whether Eq. (3)'s spectral fill factor of 0.75 has an implicit wavelength dependence.

q: How sensitive is the extrapolated 3.6 Gbit/s (12.5 GHz, 1000 mW) claim to a ±20% variation in the coherence time σ_C(λ₀, Δλ), which the paper leaves unspecified beyond 'approximated from central wavelength and respective WDM width'?
basis: σ_C enters the erf argument of Eq. (1) as sqrt(t_Δ² + σ_C²) in the denominator; for the 12.5 GHz Δλ≈0.1 nm case at λ₀=1550 nm, transform-limited FWHM gives σ_C≈22 ps, comparable to t_Δ=38 ps, so the erf is sub-unity and the optimal t_CC depends sensitively on σ_C.
next_steps: Sweep σ_C over [0.5×, 2×] transform-limited value at fixed pump/WDM and compute d(log R_s)/d(log σ_C). If it exceeds ~0.3, the 3.6 Gbit/s extrapolation is not model-robust and should be flagged as requiring an explicit coherence-time measurement per channel.

q: The 12.5 GHz n=529 scenario nominally requires ~1058 physical WDM channels across a 66 nm range, but the paper's usable Λ(λ) band drops sharply beyond ±53 nm and outer-channel contributions become negligible. Does the paper's headline 3.6 Gbit/s implicitly assume ideal outer-channel efficiency, or a pruning strategy?
basis: Our replication truncates the sum at |Δλ|≤53 nm because Λ(λ) has fallen to <5% there; the effective n_used is far less than 529. Yet the paper cites 529 channel pairs as the source of the 3.6 Gbit/s figure without explaining how outer channels contribute enough to matter.
next_steps: Reproduce Fig. 6 while explicitly logging the per-channel R_s contribution for each of the 529 pairs. Determine at what k the marginal contribution drops below 1% of the peak channel's contribution and check whether the paper's total is consistent with truncation.

q: The paper's 10-km fiber correction ('multiply by 63%') ignores pump-power reoptimization in the lossy regime. When accidentals are suppressed by loss, is there a rebalancing of P that recovers more than 63% of the loss-free rate?
basis: Our replication at fixed 400 mW finds only 40% of the loss-free rate at 10 km, because at 400 mW we are already above the pump-power optimum for the loss-free case, and losses make the accidental-vs-true crossover shift further. In principle, dropping P at 10 km could restore a higher R_s than the naive multiplication.
next_steps: Add a two-parameter optimization (P, t_CC) at each distance and compare to the constant-P linear multiplication used by the paper. Quantify the deviation as a function of L in [0, 100] km, and identify the crossover where reoptimization matters (>10% correction).

q: The paper assumes '200 MHz max SNSPD count rate' with 2% deadtime loss, but our replication shows per-channel singles routinely exceeding 250-350 MHz on central WDM pairs at 400 mW. Does the paper's 1.2 Gbit/s headline implicitly require 132 physical SNSPDs (one per party per channel) rather than a smaller detector count with multiplexing?
basis: Bare singles = B·P·Δλ·η = 4.1e6 × 400 × 0.8 × 0.19 ≈ 2.5e8 Hz per WDM channel per party, at the 100 GHz spacing. The paper's Fig. 1 shows only a few SNSPD channels, but Fig. 6 requires n=66 channel pairs to be individually detected simultaneously, which means 132 SNSPDs per party each running at ~250 MHz.
next_steps: Query recent SNSPD arrays (e.g. Photon Spot, ID Quantique, PicoQuant) for the largest available system that simultaneously delivers 80% efficiency, <100 ps jitter, and 200+ MHz per channel across 100+ channels. If no such system exists, the 1.2 Gbit/s claim depends on hardware that has not yet been demonstrated as a single integrated system --- a legitimate finding for a replication report.
